name: Dumbbell Scaption Raise

Keep the thumbs neutral and lower without swinging.

name: Standing Barbell Curl
why: A bilateral barbell curl makes elbow-flexion load and repetition progress simple to measure across training blocks.
caution: Use a grip that is comfortable for the wrists and stop the set before torso swing replaces elbow flexion.

Lower to straight arms without leaning forward.

name: Alternating Dumbbell Curl
why: Alternating arms permits focused supination and makes left-to-right strength differences easy to observe.
caution: Keep both shoulders quiet and reduce the load if the torso twists or the working elbow drifts forward.

Supinate as one dumbbell curls toward the shoulder.
Lower fully before switching arms.

name: Cable Preacher Curl
why: Preacher support limits shoulder movement while the cable maintains elbow-flexion tension near the shortened position.
caution: Align the elbows with the bench pad and avoid forcefully locking them at the bottom under cable tension.
cues: Set the bench so the upper arms lie flat on the pad.
Curl the handle without lifting the elbows.
Control the return to a comfortable near-straight arm.

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Preacher Curl
why: Single-arm preacher support isolates elbow flexion and lets each biceps train through a controlled dumbbell range.
caution: Do not relax into a forceful elbow lockout, and use the free hand to safely position the dumbbell.

Curl until the forearm approaches vertical.
Lower slowly while keeping the shoulder still.

name: Single-Arm Cable Curl
why: A unilateral cable curl supplies continuous resistance and allows precise setup for each arm.
caution: Stand far enough from the stack to maintain tension but not so far that the shoulder is pulled forward.
cues: Hold the low handle with the arm beside the torso.

Extend slowly until the biceps lengthens comfortably.

name: Incline Hammer Curl
why: The inclined bench limits momentum while a neutral grip loads the brachialis and elbow flexors through a long position.
caution: Use a moderate incline and avoid allowing the upper arms to drift behind a comfortable shoulder position.
cues: Sit back with palms facing each other.
Curl while the upper arms remain nearly vertical.
Lower fully without rotating the wrists.

name: Resistance-Band Hammer Curl
why: A neutral-grip band curl offers portable brachialis work with resistance increasing toward the top.
caution: Stand evenly on an intact band and shorten the range if the wrists cannot stay neutral.
cues: Grip the band with thumbs pointing upward.
Curl both hands while keeping elbows at the sides.
Lower smoothly without losing band tension.

name: EZ-Bar Lying Triceps Extension
why: The lying overhead arm position lengthens the long head while the EZ-bar supports measurable bilateral loading.
caution: Use safeties or a spotter, keep the wrists comfortable, and avoid turning the movement into a pullover.
cues: Hold the bar over the shoulders with elbows pointing up.
Bend the elbows to lower behind the forehead.
Extend the elbows while the upper arms stay angled back.

name: Single-Arm Overhead Dumbbell Extension
why: Unilateral overhead extension loads the triceps long head in a lengthened position and exposes side-to-side control.
caution: Use a light load and stop if the shoulder cannot stay comfortable overhead or the elbow becomes irritated.
cues: Hold one dumbbell overhead with the elbow forward.
Lower the weight behind the head by bending only the elbow.
Extend fully without arching the lower back.

name: Overhead Band Triceps Extension
why: An anchored band offers portable long-head training with rising resistance toward elbow lockout.
caution: Secure the anchor behind the body and use tension that does not pull the shoulders or spine out of position.
cues: Face away from a low anchor with hands overhead.
Keep the upper arms beside the ears.
Straighten the elbows, then return under control.

name: Reverse-Grip Cable Pressdown
why: The underhand cable grip provides a distinct pressdown option with close elbow positioning and consistent resistance.
caution: Keep the load modest because the supinated grip can be limited by wrist comfort and grip strength.
cues: Take an underhand grip with elbows at the ribs.
Extend the forearms until the elbows are straight.
Return without allowing the shoulders to roll forward.

name: Cross-Body Cable Triceps Extension
why: The cross-body cable line lets one triceps extend the elbow through a controlled path with minimal setup load.
caution: Keep the shoulder fixed and choose a handle position that does not force the wrist into an uncomfortable angle.
cues: Hold the opposite high cable across the chest.
Pin the upper arm while extending down and outward.
Pause at lockout before returning slowly.

name: JM Press
why: The hybrid close-grip press and extension permits heavy triceps loading for lifters with established barbell technique.
caution: Learn with an empty bar, use safeties, and stop if the short lowering path causes elbow or wrist discomfort.
cues: Begin with a narrow grip over the upper chest.
Lower the bar toward the chin as elbows bend forward.
Reverse the path by extending the elbows, not flaring them.

name: Barbell Wrist Curl
why: Supported barbell wrist flexion allows both forearms to train together with small, measurable load increases.
caution: Use light loads and a pain-free range; do not force the wrists into extreme extension at the bottom.
cues: Support the forearms on a bench with palms upward.
Let the bar roll toward the fingers under control.
Curl the wrists while the forearms stay planted.

name: Barbell Wrist Extension
why: A palms-down supported curl directly trains wrist extensors with a simple bilateral progression.
caution: Use a very light bar and stop if the back of the wrist or elbow becomes painful.
cues: Rest the forearms on a bench with palms down.
Lower the knuckles through a comfortable range.
Extend the wrists without lifting the forearms.

name: Dumbbell Forearm Pronation and Supination
why: Controlled forearm rotation trains pronators and supinators that conventional wrist curls do not directly challenge.
caution: Hold the dumbbell close to one end and use very little load because leverage increases quickly.
cues: Support the forearm with the elbow bent to 90 degrees.
Rotate the palm up and down through a comfortable arc.
Keep the wrist straight and move only the forearm.

name: Smith Machine Squat
why: The guided bar path provides a stable squat that supports consistent depth, foot placement, and progressive loading.
caution: Test foot position with an empty bar so the fixed path does not force the knees, hips, or back into discomfort.
cues: Place the feet slightly ahead of the bar.
Sit down between the hips while the knees track over toes.
Drive through the whole foot to stand.

name: Barbell Split Squat
why: A stationary split stance permits substantial unilateral quadriceps loading and clear barbell progression.
caution: Use rack safeties and master the unloaded stance first because balance and bar control can limit the set.
cues: Set a stable stance with both feet pointing forward.
Lower the rear knee while the front knee bends naturally.
Push through the front foot without shifting sideways.

name: Front-Foot-Elevated Dumbbell Split Squat
why: Elevating the front foot can increase available knee and hip range while dumbbells allow independent load progression.
caution: Use a low, nonslip platform and limit depth to the range where the front heel and pelvis stay controlled.
cues: Plant the whole front foot on a low step.
Descend straight down with the knee tracking over toes.
Drive up through the elevated leg without bouncing.

name: Belt Squat
why: Loading through a hip belt trains the legs deeply while reducing spinal loading and upper-body support demands.
caution: Center the belt and platform before loading, and use hand support only for balance rather than pulling upward.
cues: Stand evenly over the machine pulley or lever.
Squat between the hips with an upright torso.
Push the platform away to return to standing.

name: Bodyweight Step-Down
why: Controlled step-downs develop single-leg knee control and quadriceps strength through an easily scaled platform height.
caution: Start with a low step and use light hand support if the knee collapses inward or the pelvis drops.
cues: Stand on one leg near the edge of a step.
Lower the free heel toward the floor slowly.
Press through the stance foot without pushing off below.

name: Single-Leg Leg Extension
why: Training one leg at a time isolates knee extension and allows straightforward comparison and load selection between sides.
caution: Align the machine pivot with the knee and avoid kicking into forceful lockout, especially with knee irritation.
cues: Set the shin pad just above the ankle.
Extend one knee without lifting the hip.
Lower through the full controlled machine range.

name: Dumbbell Goblet Squat
why: A front-held dumbbell encourages an upright squat and makes depth and loading accessible with minimal equipment.
caution: Keep the weight close to the chest and reduce depth if the heels lift or the lower back rounds.
cues: Cup one dumbbell vertically at the chest.
Sit between the knees while keeping the whole foot down.
Stand tall without throwing the weight upward.

name: Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift
why: Dumbbells provide an accessible hip hinge that loads the hamstrings through a long muscle length with flexible hand placement.
caution: Stop descending when hamstring tension would make the spine round, and keep the weights close to the legs.
cues: Begin tall with softly bent knees.
Push the hips back as the dumbbells slide beside the thighs.
Stand by driving the hips forward, not leaning back.

name: Standing Cable Leg Curl
why: An ankle cuff and low cable create unilateral knee-flexion resistance without requiring a dedicated curl machine.
caution: Use stable hand support and keep the thigh vertical so hip extension does not replace the leg curl.
cues: Attach the cuff low and face the cable stack.
Bend the working knee while keeping both thighs aligned.
Lower the foot slowly without touching the stack.

name: Band Lying Leg Curl
why: A low band anchor offers portable knee-flexion training with increasing resistance as the heels approach the hips.
caution: Secure the band carefully and position far enough away that it stays tensioned without pulling the ankles abruptly.
cues: Lie face-down with the band around both ankles.
Curl the heels toward the hips without lifting the thighs.
Return slowly until the knees are nearly straight.

name: Assisted Nordic Hamstring Curl
why: Band assistance scales the demanding Nordic eccentric and helps preserve trunk alignment through a larger controlled range.
caution: Anchor the feet and band securely, pad the knees, and use enough help to prevent an uncontrolled fall.
cues: Kneel tall with the band supporting the chest.
Lower the body from the knees as one rigid line.
Use the hamstrings and band to return upright.

name: Hamstring Walkout
why: Walking the heels away from a bridge progressively lengthens the hamstrings while maintaining hip-extension tension.
caution: Take short steps and end the set if the hips drop, the lower back cramps, or the hamstrings threaten to cramp.
cues: Begin in a bridge with heels near the hips.
Walk the heels away one small step at a time.
Keep the hips lifted before walking back in.

name: Dumbbell Lateral Lunge
why: Stepping sideways loads the adductors through frontal-plane hip motion while the dumbbells provide measurable progression.
caution: Keep the planted foot flat and reduce depth if the working knee collapses inward or groin discomfort appears.
cues: Step wide while holding the weights at the sides.
Sit into the stepping hip as the other leg stays long.
Push the floor away to return to the start.

name: Side-Lying Hip Adduction
why: The side-lying position isolates the lower leg's hip adductors with no equipment and an easily controlled range.
caution: Support the head and keep the pelvis stacked; stop if lifting the leg causes groin or hip-joint pain.
cues: Cross the top foot in front of the straight lower leg.
Lift the lower leg without rolling the pelvis.
Pause briefly, then lower without relaxing completely.

name: Wide-Stance Leg Press
why: A comfortable wider stance lets the adductors assist hip extension under a stable, progressively loadable machine path.
caution: Use only a stance width the hips tolerate and stop the platform before the pelvis rolls away from the pad.
cues: Place the feet wide with knees tracking over toes.
Lower until the hips and back remain firmly supported.
Press through both feet without locking the knees hard.

name: Barbell Lateral Lunge
why: The barbell adds substantial progressive load to frontal-plane lunging and lengthened adductor work.
caution: Master the bodyweight and dumbbell versions first, use rack safeties, and avoid loading beyond stable lateral control.
cues: Set the bar securely across the upper back.
Step wide and sit into the moving-side hip.
Drive through that foot to bring the stance back together.

name: Smith Machine Hip Thrust
why: The guided bar removes horizontal balance demands while supporting repeatable, heavily loaded hip extension.
caution: Pad the bar, secure the bench, and stop at full hip extension rather than arching the lower back.
cues: Place the shoulder blades against a stable bench.
Drive the hips upward through the heels.
Finish with ribs down and shins near vertical.

name: Bodyweight Glute Bridge
why: The floor bridge teaches hip extension and pelvic control with no equipment before external load is added.
caution: Shorten the range if the lower back takes over, and move the feet until the hamstrings remain comfortable.
cues: Lie with the feet flat and knees bent.
Tuck the pelvis gently before lifting the hips.
Pause in a straight shoulder-to-knee line.

name: Barbell Glute Bridge
why: The floor-limited bridge supports heavy glute loading with a shorter range and less bench setup than a hip thrust.
caution: Use a thick bar pad and avoid bouncing the plates or overextending the lower back at lockout.
cues: Position the padded bar across the hip crease.
Drive through the heels to lift the hips.
Lower until the pelvis lightly meets the floor.

name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge
why: Removing one foot increases unilateral hip-extension demand and reveals differences in pelvic control without added load.
caution: Keep the pelvis level and switch to the bilateral version if the hamstrings cramp or the back extends.
cues: Plant one foot while the other knee stays lifted.
Drive the stance heel down to raise the hips.
Keep both hip bones level through the repetition.

name: Feet-Elevated Glute Bridge
why: Elevating the feet changes hip and knee angles and increases the usable bridge range for glute and posterior-chain work.
caution: Use a nonslip bench and choose a height that does not cause hamstring cramping or pelvic instability.
cues: Place both heels securely on the bench.
Brace before driving the hips upward.
Lower slowly while the feet remain planted.

name: Dumbbell Long-Stride Walking Lunge
why: Longer walking steps increase hip flexion and glute contribution while dumbbells permit steady progressive loading.
caution: Use a clear walkway and shorten the stride if balance, knee tracking, or hip comfort deteriorates.
cues: Step long enough for the front shin to stay controlled.
Lower the rear knee while leaning forward only slightly.
Drive through the front heel into the next step.

name: Deficit Dumbbell Reverse Lunge
why: A low front-foot platform increases hip range in a reverse lunge and creates a strong lengthened glute challenge.
caution: Start with a very low deficit and light loads; stop if the stance foot shifts or the front hip pinches.
cues: Stand fully on a low stable platform.
Step back and lower straight down under control.
Push through the elevated foot to return.

name: Banded Hip Thrust
why: A band anchored across the hips provides portable hip-extension resistance that increases toward lockout.
caution: Secure both sides of the band and the bench before starting, and protect the hips from concentrated band pressure.
cues: Set the shoulder blades against the bench.
Drive the knees slightly outward as the hips rise.
Hold full extension without flaring the ribs.

name: Standing Band Hip Extension
why: A low anchored band isolates hip extension in standing with little setup and clear unilateral control.
caution: Hold stable support and use light tension so the movement comes from the hip rather than the lower back.
cues: Loop the band around one ankle and face the anchor.
Move the straight leg backward from the hip.
Return slowly without leaning the torso forward.

name: Cable Reverse Lunge
why: Front-loaded cable tension provides counterbalance and continuous resistance through a glute-focused reverse lunge.
caution: Use a secure handle and remain clear of the stack; select a load that does not pull the torso forward.
cues: Hold the low cable at the chest and step back.
Lower until the front hip and knee bend comfortably.
Drive through the front foot while resisting the cable.

name: Side Plank Hip Abduction
why: Combining a side plank with top-leg abduction challenges the glute medius while the pelvis resists lateral collapse.
caution: Use a bent-knee side plank first and stop if the supporting shoulder or outer hip cannot maintain alignment.
cues: Set a stable side plank with hips stacked.
Lift the top leg without turning the toes upward.
Keep the pelvis high as the leg lowers.

name: Standing Band Hip Abduction
why: A low band provides simple standing resistance for hip abduction and single-leg pelvic control.
caution: Hold a support and use a light band so the torso does not lean away to create extra range.
cues: Anchor the band across the body at ankle height.
Move the outside leg laterally with the toes forward.
Return slowly while keeping the stance hip level.

name: Cable Hip Hike
why: Low cable resistance makes frontal-plane pelvic elevation progressively loadable for the stance-side hip abductors.
caution: Use a small controlled range and stable hand support; do not bend the trunk sideways to move the cable.
cues: Stand on a low step with the cable on the free-side ankle.
Lower the free side of the pelvis slightly.
Hike that hip up while the stance knee stays soft.

name: Standing Machine Hip Abduction
why: The supported standing machine offers stable unilateral hip-abduction loading with simple adjustments and progression.
caution: Align the pad with the outside of the thigh and keep the pelvis square instead of rotating for more range.
cues: Brace the torso against the machine support.
Move the working leg outward from the hip.
Pause briefly before returning to neutral.

name: Banded Side-Lying Hip Abduction
why: Adding a loop band makes side-lying abduction progressively harder near the top while the torso remains supported.
caution: Place the band above the knees if ankle placement disrupts control, and avoid rolling the pelvis backward.
cues: Lie with the hips stacked and band under light tension.
Raise the top leg with the toes facing forward.
Lower slowly without letting the band snap the legs together.

name: Single-Leg Wall-Press Isometric
why: Pressing the lifted knee into a wall creates an isometric demand on both hips and trains pelvic stability in standing.
caution: Stand close enough to the wall to remain upright and use fingertip support if balance is uncertain.
cues: Stand beside a wall and lift the wall-side knee.
Press that knee into the wall without leaning.
Keep the stance hip level and breathe steadily.

name: Hanging Straight-Leg Raise
why: The long straight-leg lever makes posterior pelvic tilt and controlled trunk flexion substantially more demanding than a knee raise.
caution: Begin with bent knees if the pelvis cannot curl without swinging, and stop if hanging irritates the shoulders or grip.
cues: Hang actively with the shoulders away from the ears.
Raise straight legs while curling the pelvis upward.
Lower slowly without letting the body swing.

name: Lying Straight-Leg Raise
why: The floor-supported long-lever raise trains abdominal control as the legs move away from and back toward the torso.
caution: Bend the knees or shorten the lowering range if the lower back lifts or discomfort develops.
cues: Lie flat and gently press the lower ribs down.
Raise both legs without using momentum.
Lower only as far as the back stays supported.

name: Cable Reverse Crunch
why: A low cable attached to the ankles progressively loads posterior pelvic tilt rather than only moving the hips.
caution: Use a padded cuff and light load, keep clear of the stack, and stop if the attachment pulls on the knees or lower back.
cues: Lie facing away from a low cable with knees bent.
Curl the pelvis toward the ribs as the knees come in.
Unroll slowly until the hips return to the floor.

name: V-Up
why: Simultaneously lifting the trunk and straight legs creates a demanding bodyweight flexion pattern through a large range.
caution: Use a tuck-up variation if straight-leg repetitions require jerking, neck pulling, or painful lower-back flexion.
cues: Start long with arms overhead and legs together.
Lift the torso and legs toward a balanced V.
Lower both halves under control without dropping.

name: Bodyweight Crunch
why: A short controlled spinal-flexion range gives beginners a simple way to train the rectus abdominis without equipment.
caution: Keep the hands away from pulling the head and use a small range if repeated flexion is uncomfortable.
cues: Lie with feet planted and fingertips beside the temples.
Lift the shoulder blades by bringing ribs toward the pelvis.
Pause, then lower the upper back slowly.

name: Dumbbell Side Bend
why: A single dumbbell directly loads lateral trunk flexion through a simple standing range.
caution: Use one weight rather than counterbalancing with two, and avoid combining the bend with rotation or forward flexion.
cues: Hold one dumbbell at the side and stand tall.
Lower it a short distance by bending toward the loaded side.
Use the opposite obliques to return to neutral.

name: Cable Side Bend
why: A low cable supplies consistent unilateral resistance for controlled lateral trunk flexion.
caution: Keep the hips square and use a modest range so momentum or pelvic shifting does not dominate the movement.
cues: Stand side-on with the low handle in the near hand.
Bend slightly toward the cable without rotating.
Return upright against the cable's pull.

name: Dumbbell Suitcase March
why: Marching with one-sided load trains the obliques to resist lateral flexion while balance changes on every step.
caution: Use a clear area or march in place, and reduce the load if the torso leans or the stance becomes unstable.
cues: Hold one dumbbell beside the hip and stand tall.
Lift one knee at a time without leaning toward the weight.
Keep the shoulders level and steps quiet.

name: Plank Shoulder Tap
why: Removing one hand from a plank creates alternating anti-rotation demand while the trunk maintains a stable line.
caution: Widen the feet or use an elevated surface if the pelvis rotates, and stop if the supporting wrists are uncomfortable.
cues: Set a high plank with feet slightly wider than the hips.
Tap the opposite shoulder without shifting body weight abruptly.
Alternate sides while keeping the pelvis square.

name: Side-Plank Cable Row
why: Combining a side plank with a unilateral row challenges lateral trunk stability against changing cable force.
caution: Master a stable side plank first and select a light load that does not pull the supporting shoulder out of position.
cues: Face the low cable in a supported side plank.
Row the handle while keeping the hips stacked.
Extend the arm without letting the torso rotate.

name: Band Pallof Press
why: A securely anchored band offers portable anti-rotation training with an easily adjusted stance and lever length.
caution: Inspect the band and anchor, and step closer if the torso cannot remain square as the arms extend.
cues: Stand side-on and hold the band at the sternum.
Press the hands forward without turning toward the anchor.
Pause at full reach, then return to the chest.

name: Body Saw
why: Sliding the body backward from a forearm plank lengthens the anti-extension lever and progressively challenges deep trunk control.
caution: Use a small range on a low-friction surface and stop when the lower back begins to extend or shoulders become uncomfortable.
cues: Set a forearm plank with feet on sliders or a towel.
Glide the whole body backward from the shoulders.
Pull forward while keeping ribs and pelvis stacked.

name: Bird-Dog Dumbbell Row
why: Rowing from a three-point quadruped base adds meaningful anti-rotation demand to contralateral trunk and hip stability.
caution: Begin without load and use a very light dumbbell; stop if the supporting wrist, knee, or lower back loses position.
cues: Set one knee and the opposite hand on a bench or floor.
Extend the free leg while rowing with the free arm.
Keep the pelvis square throughout the row.

name: Standing Cable Anti-Extension Pressdown
why: Pressing a high cable down with straight arms trains the trunk to resist extension as the resistance tries to lift the ribs.
caution: Use a load that allows a neutral spine and avoid turning the movement into a lat pulldown by bending the elbows.
cues: Face away from a high cable with arms angled forward.
Brace the ribs over the pelvis.
Press the handle toward the thighs without arching.

name: Dead-Bug Heel Tap
why: Alternating heel taps provide a clear beginner progression for maintaining trunk position while the legs move.
caution: Shorten the reach if the lower back lifts, and support the head if holding it up causes neck fatigue.
cues: Lie with hips and knees bent to 90 degrees.
Lower one heel toward the floor while exhaling.
Return and alternate without losing the abdominal brace.

name: Dumbbell Front-Rack March
why: A front-rack load challenges the trunk to stay stacked while alternating single-leg support during marching.
caution: Use lighter dumbbells than a carry and stop if the wrists, shoulders, or lower back cannot hold the rack position.
cues: Hold both dumbbells at the shoulders with elbows forward.
March one knee at a time without leaning backward.
Keep the ribs down and each footfall controlled.

name: Standing Dumbbell Calf Raise
why: Holding dumbbells makes bilateral straight-knee plantar flexion easy to load without a dedicated machine.
caution: Use stable support if balance limits the set and avoid bouncing rapidly through the bottom stretch.
cues: Stand tall with dumbbells at the sides.
Rise onto the balls of both feet with knees straight.
Pause at the top before lowering the heels fully.

name: Standing Cable Calf Raise
why: A low cable provides adjustable loading while allowing a full heel drop and controlled straight-knee calf raise.
caution: Keep the cable close to the body and use free-hand support so the stack does not pull balance backward.
cues: Hold the low handle near the hip and stand on a step.
Lower the heels while keeping the knees straight.
Push through the forefeet to rise as high as controlled.

name: Single-Leg Leg Press Calf Raise
why: The leg press stabilizes the body while one straight knee performs progressively loaded plantar flexion.
caution: Keep the safety stops engaged and the forefoot fully on the platform so it cannot slip during the heel drop.
cues: Place one forefoot low on the platform.
Keep the knee straight as the heel lowers.
Press the platform away using only the ankle.

name: Bodyweight Step Heel Drop
why: A step permits a controlled calf stretch and full bodyweight plantar-flexion range with simple progression to one leg.
caution: Hold a rail and use a stable step; shorten the bottom range if the Achilles tendon or foot becomes painful.
cues: Stand with the balls of both feet on the step edge.
Lower the heels slowly below the step.
Rise to the toes without bending the knees.

name: Jump Rope
why: Repeated low hops train elastic ankle stiffness and calf endurance in a rhythmic conditioning pattern distinct from slow raises.
caution: Begin with short bouts on a forgiving surface and avoid jumping if impact aggravates the feet, Achilles tendons, or knees.
cues: Keep the jumps low and land softly on the forefeet.
Turn the rope mainly from the wrists.
Maintain a tall posture and steady rhythm.

name: Bent-Knee Leg Press Calf Raise
why: Holding the knees bent on the leg press reduces gastrocnemius contribution and makes soleus-focused plantar flexion progressively loadable.
caution: Use light loads, maintain the knee angle, and keep the forefeet securely on the platform with safety stops set.
cues: Set the knees in a comfortable fixed bend.
Lower the heels without letting the knees straighten.
Press through the forefeet while holding the same knee angle.

name: Standing Toe Raise
why: Lifting the forefeet while standing trains ankle dorsiflexion and tibialis-anterior endurance without equipment.
caution: Use wall support and keep the heels planted; stop if the front of the ankle pinches or balance becomes uncertain.
cues: Lean the upper back lightly against a wall.
Keep both heels down as the toes lift.
Lower the forefeet slowly without relaxing completely.
